newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Crown prince Klima to become Austrian chancellor.
newsitem.headline: Crown prince Klima to become Austrian chancellor.

text.p: Austrian Finance Minister Viktor Klima, who on Saturday was chosen to succeed Chancellor Franz Vranitzky after his surprise resignation, was long regarded as the "crown prince" in Austria's political hierarchy.

The 49-year-old Social Democrat scored his biggest victory to date when he sealed the sale of flagship bank Creditanstalt to rival Bank Austria last weekend, closing Europe's longest privatisation against strong opposition from the conservative People's Party, the junior coalition partner.

Observers say the drawn-out battle with the conservatives over who would win control over the country's number two bank finally gave heir-apparent Klima the political stature to take over from Vranitzky, his close confidant and friend.
"Klima's image has gained substantially from the sale of Creditanstalt," said Hannes Androsch, one-time Social Democrat Finance Minister and vice chancellor.
Political infighting over the sale of Creditanstalt had driven a wedge between the two coalition partners and nearly forced a government collapse.
The finance minister has not made any public appearance since announcing the deal after 11 hours of crisis talks between coalition leaders last weekend.

Sources inside the Social Democratic Party said he was not present at Saturday's two-hour emergency session of party leaders, who accepted Vranitzky's resignation and his choice of Klima as Austria's eighth chancellor since World War Two.

Klima is widely expected to bring much-needed charm and savvy to the Austrian chancellery after Vranitzky's tenure at the helm of government, which many observers say was marked by a combination of political professionalism and blandness.

Klima, who was previously minister for transport and communications, was appointed as finance minister in January 1996 after the resignation of Andreas Staribacher, a politically inexperienced tax accountant.
Chain-smoking Klima entered Austria's political scene in December 1992 after a long career at oil and energy firm OMV AG, the country's biggest industrial group.

During his three years at the ministry for transport and state industry, he oversaw the successful privatisation of a roster of state-owned companies, including chip maker Austria Mikro Systeme and engineering group VA Technologie AG.
Analysts said Klima's trademark combination of toughness and charm helped him win over some of the most stubborn opponents of privatisation within his own party ranks.
Klima has largely avoided the public spotlight, but repeatedly denied he had plans to take over from Vranitzky, saying he would prefer to return to industry instead.
Insiders say Klima promised his second wife, whom he married two years ago, and his two grown children that he will leave the political arena by the year 2000.
"Once I leave politics, I don't want to become a state industry manager, I want to build up my own company. Nothing big, just something that belongs to me," he has said.
Voter surveys show Klima has a high profile with the Austrian electorate and ranks among the Alpine republic's most popular politicians.
According to a snap poll conducted by News after the sale of Creditanstalt, 54 percent of Austrians believe Klima would make a good chancellor.
"I'm happy about my popular support, but it can always drop," Klima told weekly magazine Profil last week.
